analysis.one_liner: Lets students sue colleges in court instead of forced arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill would have restored students' right to sue their colleges in court, but it was referred to a Senate committee in October 2023 and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop colleges that take federal student aid from forcing students to sign away their day in court. Enrollment agreements could no longer require students to settle disputes in private arbitration, waive jury trials, or give up the right to join class-action lawsuits against the school. It took effect one year after passage.
analysis.who_benefits: Students and former students — including borrowers who feel they were misled about their degree or its value — would regain the ability to sue their college in court and to band together in class-action suits, where individual claims too small to litigate alone can be combined. This matters most at schools that currently use arbitration clauses, especially for-profit colleges.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students suing colleges over fraud or disputes

how_it_helps.text: Students could no longer be required to agree to arbitration, limits on jury trials, choice-of-law restrictions, or venue restrictions as a condition of enrolling, and mandatory arbitration clauses in enrollment agreements would be unenforceable.

Any college participating in federal student aid would have to commit, as a program condition, not to restrict students' ability to pursue claims in court individually or with others — putting enforcement teeth behind the rule through the Higher Education Act.

The practical effect is to reopen class-action lawsuits. Class actions are how claims worth a few hundred or few thousand dollars per person — common in student disputes over fees, credits, or misleading recruitment — can be heard at all; forced arbitration typically blocks them.

analysis.who_pays: Colleges and universities, which would face more lawsuits and lose arbitration as a cheaper, private way to resolve disputes; some costs could be passed to students through tuition. Arbitration providers would lose a slice of their market.

drawbacks.text: Colleges argue that arbitration is faster and cheaper than court for everyone, and that restoring litigation — especially class actions — would raise their legal costs, costs that could be passed on to students through tuition or fees.

Class-action lawsuits can generate large attorney fees while delivering small individual recoveries, so some students might have done better in one-on-one arbitration than as a small slice of a class settlement; an honest supporter would acknowledge the remedy is not uniformly better for every student.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gain to students is real and structural: forced arbitration and class-action waivers are exactly the tools that make claims against a large institution impractical for an individual, so restoring court access changes the balance of power between a student and a school. The costs are genuine but modest — more litigation for colleges, some possible cost-shifting to tuition — and are the ordinary price of enforceable legal rights. On balance the benefits to students outweigh the costs, though the bill's one-size carve-out could have been tuned to preserve low-cost individual arbitration for students who prefer it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate's education committee the day it was introduced and sat there, without a hearing or vote, until Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Dick Durbin introduced the bill on October 24, 2023, joined by eight Democratic colleagues — Blumenthal, Booker, Fetterman, Hirono, Markey, Reed, Warren, and Whitehouse.

The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions — the standard first step that sends a bill to the committee with jurisdiction over it.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote. The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Colleges that use mandatory arbitration and class-action waivers in their enrollment agreements — for-profit college chains most of all — kept those tools, because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Sen. Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar colleges from forcing students into arbitration and limiting their right to sue.

for.name: Sens. Blumenthal, Booker, Fetterman, Hirono, Markey, Reed, Warren, and Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors at introduction; no Republican joined.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair Bernie Sanders, D-VT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it; the bill died in committee.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None supported the bill, leaving it with no cross-party base of support to pressure committee leadership for floor time.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican joined, so the bill never had the bipartisan support that typically gets a Senate bill out of committee.

industries.note: For-profit schools are the heaviest users of mandatory arbitration and class-action waivers in enrollment contracts, which have shielded them from group lawsuits by students alleging misleading recruitment or worthless degrees. The bill would strip that shield from any school taking federal aid, exposing them to court and class actions.

Many mainstream universities also write arbitration and dispute-limitation clauses into enrollment agreements; the bill would force all aid-participating institutions to give up those terms, though most face far less litigation risk than for-profit chains.
Commercial arbitration firms would lose the segment of cases arising from college enrollment contracts, one slice of a market built on mandatory arbitration clauses.

Attorneys who bring class actions against schools would regain a workable business model, since students' small individual claims become viable only when grouped; their gain comes from the same mechanism that restores students' access to court.
